Alexander the Great. Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, was a military genius who created the largest contiguous empire of the ancient world before his death at thirty-two. By conquering the Persian Empire and extending Macedonian rule from Greece to Egypt to the borders of India, he fundamentally reshaped the political and cultural landscape of three continents. His conquests inaugurated the Hellenistic era, centuries of Greek cultural dominance in Asia and the Near East, and made him history's archetypal conqueror, studied by military strategists for over two thousand years.

Born in three hundred fifty-six BCE in Pella, the capital of Macedon, Alexander was the son of King Philip II, one of ancient Greece's great military reformers. He was tutored by the philosopher Aristotle, who shaped his intellectual outlook and instilled in him a love of Greek culture and learning, which he spread throughout his conquered territories. He became king at twenty after his father's assassination in three hundred thirty-six BCE, acting with brutal decisiveness to secure his throne by executing potential rivals and re-subjugating Greek city-states that immediately rebelled. He inherited the Macedonian phalanx, a revolutionary infantry formation perfected by his father, which became the instrument of his conquests.

Alexander crossed into Asia Minor in three hundred thirty-four BCE with a relatively small force of around thirty-five thousand men and destroyed the Persian satrap's army at the Granicus River, establishing himself as a serious threat to Persian rule. He defeated the Persian king Darius III at the Battle of Issus in three hundred thirty-three BCE in southern Anatolia, a stunning tactical victory where Alexander's cavalry broke the Persian center and forced Darius to flee the battlefield. He conquered Tyre in three hundred thirty-two BCE, a heavily fortified island city, through siege and engineering mastery, demonstrating his versatility beyond pitched battles.

Alexander entered Egypt where he was crowned pharaoh and proclaimed the son of the god Amun, lending divine sanction to his rule in the eyes of his Egyptian subjects. He met and decisively defeated Darius III again at Gaugamela in three hundred thirty-one BCE, near modern-day Iraq, effectively ending Persian imperial power and making Alexander master of the Near East. He pursued the conquest eastward, took Babylon, Susa, and Persepolis burning it in celebration, seized the legendary wealth of the Persian treasury, and pushed into Central Asia and India.

He reached the Indus Valley and won a major victory at the Hydaspes River in three hundred twenty-six BCE against King Porus and his elephant army, a battle his own soldiers regarded as nearly his greatest challenge. He wished to continue east to the Ganges, but his exhausted and homesick army mutinied and refused to advance further, forcing Alexander to halt his conquests. He died in Babylon in three hundred twenty-three BCE, likely of fever possibly malaria or typhoid, at age thirty-two, leaving an empire he had ruled for only thirteen years.

Alexander never lost a pitched battle despite frequently facing numerically superior forces. His victories turned on his ability to read the enemy's weak point and deliver a cavalry strike with perfect timing. He pioneered a new kind of warfare combining heavy cavalry, light cavalry, infantry, and siege craft in a coordinated system. His tactics remained the model for armies for centuries. He founded over seventy cities throughout his empire, many named Alexandria, most famously Alexandria in Egypt, which became centers of Greek culture and trade.

He married Roxana, a Bactrian princess, and encouraged his troops to marry local women, integrating Greek and Persian cultures and creating the mixed Greco-Oriental Hellenistic civilization. Alexander stands at the threshold between the ancient world and the medieval. His conquests did not establish a durable state; his empire fragmented immediately after his death into the kingdoms of his generals. But they accomplished something more lasting: the Hellenization of Asia and the Near East for centuries. Greek language, art, and ideas became the prestigious cultural medium of the entire eastern Mediterranean and western Asia. The resulting Hellenistic era saw the greatest flowering of Greek science, mathematics, and philosophy, with Alexandria in Egypt becoming the intellectual hub of the world.

His legend became the gold standard for the ambitious young warrior-king. He was revered by the Romans, studied obsessively by Renaissance military theorists, and invoked as the model for everything from Napoleon to modern military academies. His teacher Aristotle's methods of classification and observation made their way into Islamic and medieval European science through the Hellenistic libraries Alexander's cities created. Few individuals have shaped history so directly and on such a grand scale, and fewer still achieved it at such a young age.
